## Status rules

`PENDING_CHECK` is not a finding. `CONFIRMED` requires a current reproduction (or conclusive static evidence where execution is inappropriate), root cause, reachability and source. `FIXED_BASELINE` requires current code/test evidence, not ancestry alone. `FIXED_HERE` additionally records the repair commit and red/green verification. `LIMITATION` is a truthful model/product boundary. `BLOCKED_EXTERNAL` names the missing owner/data/environment input. Dormant but callable library bugs remain bugs, separately labelled.

DNS (getaddrinfo) is also unbounded. _run_owned_thread deliberately keeps the permit until the worker exits. A slow upstream therefore pins the 2 realtime (or 2 tile) permits, and every other request gets 503 saturated. |

| P038 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Every /solar/physics poll is a cold full PFSS solve (9-15 s): spawn-per-request children discard the PFSS cache and the exact-JD cache key never repeats; under load the 18 s backend / 20 s client deadlines fail more than half the polls — The frontend polls GET /solar/physics every 30 s with jd_tdb=simState.julianDate.toFixed(8). At the default +4 d/s the epoch is different on every poll. The backend runs each request in a fresh multiprocessing 'spawn' child (SupervisedProcessRunner), so the PFSS cache (PFSSManager._cache, keyed by a synthetic snapshot id equal to the exact JD) starts empty each time. Even in-process the key misses for a +1e-8 d change. Every request therefore re-traces 120 field lines (trace_field_batch is about 87% of the time) and rebuilds the WSA map. The cost is 9-10 s on an idle 32-core box and 12-21 s under moderate load. The limits are SOLAR_PHYSICS_COMPUTE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=18 on the server and a 20 s abort in the client. The next request is scheduled 30 s after the previous one started, so each tab keeps a compute worker busy about 60% of the time. With 2 workers plus a queue of 2, about 3 open tabs saturate the backend. |

| P033 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Backend corona vectors are Z-north but every frontend consumer reads them as Y-north: physics-driven sunspots and coronal loops are drawn at the wrong latitudes (54% beyond 40 deg, up to 76 deg) and tumble about an axis 90 deg from the rendered spin axis — _vector_from_lat_lon puts sin(lat) in z, and _region_polarity_dirs rotates active regions about z, so every corona feature (base_dir, paired_dir, arc) uses z as solar north. The frontend never converts axes. collectPhysicsDrivenSunspotGroups computes lat=asin(center[1]) and lon=atan2(center[2],center[0]), which is Y-north. The coronal-loop and eruption groups are children of the Sun's spinGroup, whose local spin axis is BODY_LOCAL_SPIN_AXIS=(0,1,0), and updateBodyRotations spins them about local Y. Backend north therefore lands on the rendered solar equator. The backend's differential-rotation advance (about backend z) is composed with the frontend spin (about local Y), so features tumble over the rendered poles and rotation is applied twice. The Parker-spiral group is parented to the un-tilted node instead (backend z = world Z), so the spiral and the loops also disagree with each other. |

| P002 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Unauthenticated local-profile POST /benchmark/accuracy/report overwrites the owner's tracked my-notes/*.md; no Host/Origin check makes it reachable via DNS rebinding — BENCHMARK_REPORTS_DIR is PROJECT_ROOT/my-notes, which holds 74 git-tracked owner notes. _resolve_benchmark_report_path only requires the target to be a .md file under my-notes, and allow_overwrite=true makes generate_accuracy_report call path.write_text(). The default 'local' profile has no authentication. No middleware validates the Host header (there is no TrustedHostMiddleware), and nothing checks the Origin of same-origin requests. So a DNS-rebinding page (Origin == Host == attacker:8042, resolving to 127.0.0.1) or any local process can send application/json and replace any note. Cross-site simple requests are blocked (text/plain gets 422, preflight gets 400), so the routes in are rebinding or local access. |
| P009 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Local profile has no CSRF/Host defence: any web page can make the backend write/overwrite .md files (and nested dirs) under my-notes/ via POST /benchmark/accuracy/report — In SOLAR_SECURITY_PROFILE=local (the default) every route is unauthenticated, and the only cross-site barrier is CORS, which never blocks a 'simple' request. A no-cors fetch with a typeless Blob body sends NO Content-Type header, so the browser sends no preflight. Whether FastAPI then parses the body as JSON depends only on its strict_content_type default. fastapi 0.141.1 (the CI pin) rejects it with 422. backend/requirements.txt allows fastapi>=0.100.0, and 0.115.12 parses the body and runs the endpoint. The endpoint takes output_path (any relative .md path under my-notes; parent dirs are created via mkdir(parents=True)) and allow_overwrite=true. Independently of FastAPI version, there is no TrustedHost/Host check, so a DNS-rebinding page (same-origin after rebinding, application/json allowed) reaches the same write primitive. |

| P005 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Every client disconnect during owned solar/trajectory work logs a ~65-line ERROR 'Exception in ASGI application' traceback plus 'Future exception was never retrieved' — _RequestOwnerDisconnected subclasses asyncio.CancelledError and is re-raised out of the endpoint. Starlette's ServerErrorMiddleware only handles Exception, so it reaches uvicorn's run_asgi `except BaseException`, which logs an ERROR with the full traceback and tries to send a 500 on a dead socket. Separately, SupervisedProcessRunner.run() awaits asyncio.shield(wrap_future(f)). After the owner cancels, the inner wrapped future later completes with ProcessCancelled and is never awaited, so asyncio logs 'Future exception was never retrieved' at garbage collection. |
| P088 | this-audit status-incidental-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | UNVERIFIED | Client aborts of /solar/physics log as unhandled 'Exception in ASGI application' tracebacks plus an unretrieved ProcessCancelled future — _run_request_owned_process raises _RequestOwnerDisconnected (an asyncio.CancelledError subclass) out of the route when the peer disconnects; nothing catches it, so uvicorn logs it as an application exception. The supervisor future's ProcessCancelled exception is never retrieved, so asyncio also logs 'Future exception was never retrieved'. Each frontend abort (Sun focus/epoch change aborting an in-flight fetch) therefore writes ~65 lines of ERROR traceback and makes normal cancellations look like server crashes. |

| P006 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Solar worker children have no parent-death guard; SIGKILL/OOM of the API process leaves them computing to completion — The hard deadline and cancellation live only in the parent's supervisor thread. daemon=True only matters for an orderly interpreter exit. If the parent is SIGKILLed (OOM killer, kill -9, a crashed reloader), the spawn child keeps running its model build until it finishes, then fails on the broken pipe. A restarted server immediately admits K new children, briefly doubling CPU use. |
| P008 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Documented `python server.py` launch makes every solar spawn child re-import the whole API server (and the reload worker import it twice) — multiprocessing 'spawn' re-imports a file-based __main__ as __mp_main__ in each child. Under `python -m uvicorn` the main module is uvicorn.__main__, which is skipped. Under `python backend/server.py` (the module's own __main__ block), every solar child imports server.py: the FastAPI app, providers, executors and runner. That breaks the worker's stated contract of being import-safe 'without importing the API server'. With reload=True, the uvicorn spawn worker also holds server twice (as __mp_main__ and as server). |
| P003 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | dev:full 'network' gate exposes the unauthenticated Vite dev server (whole working tree incl. my-notes, source; Vite 7.3.1 file-read CVEs) on the LAN, while the shipped UI cannot authenticate to the network-profile backend — parseDevFullConfig treats SOLAR_SECURITY_PROFILE=network as enough to bind a non-loopback --host, and buildFrontendArgs passes that same host to `vite`, the dev server. The network profile only authenticates the FastAPI backend. The Vite dev server has no auth and serves every file under the project root (my-notes/*.md, agent-notes, backend source). The installed vite 7.3.1 is also inside GHSA-p9ff-h696-f583 (arbitrary file read via the dev-server WebSocket) and GHSA-v2wj-q39q-566r (server.fs.deny bypass). Meanwhile the frontend never sends X-API-Key or Authorization (no occurrence in src/ outside tests), and the network CORS default is deny-all, so every UI backend call returns 401. The gate therefore produces a broken UI plus an open file server. |
| P010 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | One client request with an out-of-coverage epoch trips the process-wide Horizons outage breaker, denying Horizons Lambert to every client for 30-60 s — TrajectoryLambertRequest accepts any FiniteFloat departure/arrival JD, and nothing on the Horizons path range-checks it before the outbound call (jd=1e15 and jd=-1e9 both reach urlopen). Horizons answers an out-of-coverage epoch with HTTP 200 + {"error":...} or with a 4xx. _parse_horizons_payload (or the HTTPError branch) maps that to EphemerisProtocolError. EphemerisProtocolError is in _PROVIDER_WIDE_FAILURES, so the single-flight owner installs the module-global _SHARED_PROVIDER_OUTAGES['horizons'] for 30-60 s. Every later Horizons request from any client is refused without an outbound attempt. A caller-input error is treated as a provider outage. The existing test asserts this global circuit for protocol errors, and no test distinguishes caller-input rejections. |
| P011 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Solar physics admission: the per-identity rate limit (36/min) is about 2.5x the global worker capacity, so one client (or a cross-site GET) can keep the shipped UI's /solar/physics at 503 saturated — Each /solar/physics call spawns a fresh 'spawn' child; the pool is 2 workers plus 2 queued, shared globally. Measured service time here is 6-13 s, so capacity is roughly 10-20 calls/min. SOLAR_PHYSICS_RATE_LIMIT_PER_WINDOW still admits 36/min per identity, and no identity has a fair share of workers. In local profile the route is a CORS-simple GET. |
| P012 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | /solar/realtime/aia-tile with client-chosen jd_tdb (and /solar/realtime?force_refresh=true) bypass the snapshot cache and fan out to 7-8 upstream requests per call, including irrelevant current SWPC feeds — The tile endpoint accepts any finite jd_tdb (no validity window, unlike /solar/physics). latest(jd_tdb) keys a 16-entry LRU on the raw float, so every new value misses the cache. _fetch_snapshot_with_deadline then refetches SWPC wind and mag (current data, unrelated to a historical epoch), SILSO, 5 Helioviewer getClosestImage calls and the tile. In local profile, GET /solar/realtime?force_refresh=true does the same with no key (network profile forbids it). |
| P059 | this-audit status-incidental-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | UNVERIFIED | Extreme finite departure_jd (±1e308) on /trajectory/plan and /mission/plan returns unhandled 500 (TrajectoryInputError not mapped) — FiniteFloat accepts 1e308. | P047 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | All URA184 rows lead Horizons by a common 0.0100 d at their own 2025 epoch, and their 4-digit periods lose phase within months — At epochTdb (2025-01-01.0 TDB, parsed correctly as JD 2460676.5) every URA184 moon is ahead of Horizons by an angle proportional to its mean motion. That is a common ~0.0100 d (14.4 min) time offset, i.e. a systematic convention mismatch rather than random rounding. On top of that, periodDays has only 4 decimals, which adds tens of degrees of drift per year for these 0.33-0.92 d orbits. Cordelia avoided this only because it was moved to a Chebyshev fit. |

The Laplace-frame lambda at J2000 matches Horizons to within 0.04-0.09 deg, so the along-track drift comes from the propagated mean motion or secular rates. verify:moon-frames does not cover these moons. Dormant because moons are not rendered. This is a sub-case of MOON-012. |

| P035 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Active-region bipoles break both Hale's and Joy's laws: Cycle-25 hemisphere polarity sign is inverted, the positive footpoint always leads in both hemispheres, and the mean tilt puts the leading spot poleward — (1) Hale sign. Line 245 asserts 'Cycle 25 is odd: north leading is negative', and _region_polarity_dirs sets north_leading_sign=-1 for odd cycles. In the Babcock-Leighton/Hale picture, a hemisphere's polar field at cycle onset has the sign of its new-cycle leading polarity. WSO shows the north polar field positive at Cycle 25 onset (2019) and negative at Cycle 24 onset (2009), so odd cycles lead positive in the north and the code's sign is inverted. (2) Geometry. positive_dir = center + axis*tan(sep/2) with axis = east*cos(tilt) + north*sin(tilt), where 'east' = d/dlon is the direction of rotation (lon += omega*t). The positive footpoint is therefore always the rotation-leading one in both hemispheres, so opposite hemispheric leading polarities cannot exist, and source_role contradicts the geometry for about half the loops. | P034 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | /solar/physics: 'ultra' fidelity is accepted but cannot finish inside the 18 s deadline, and the deadline starts at submit, so queued requests (including the shipped 'high' request) time out. Two ultra calls deny the solar feature to every client — Each request spawns a fresh worker that builds a new SolarCoronaPhysicsModel, so its PFSSCache is always cold. The synthetic PFSS key includes the exact JD, so a cache would not hit even in-process. PFSS field-line tracing dominates the cost: pfss_tracing.trace_field_batch takes 16.6 of 17.0 s in cProfile at 'high'. 'ultra' (180 lines, lmax 15) needs more than the 18 s default and the 19 s hard maximum. SupervisedProcessRunner.submit fixes absolute_deadline = now + 18 s before the job waits for one of the 2 workers. A queued job therefore starts with whatever time is left, burns CPU and is killed. With 2 workers and a queue of 2, two ultra requests (each a 503 anyway) block everyone, and any request queued behind a ~11 s 'high' job is guaranteed to fail. No test asserts that each advertised fidelity fits the deadline. |

| P015 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Every shipped 'high' solar request recomputes PFSS from scratch (~10 s): PFSSCache lives in a fresh per-request spawn process, and display lines use the per-point scalar tracer (5-6x slower than the existing bit-identical batch tracer) — trace_field_lines loops over the seeds and calls trace_field() for each. Its ScalarAdapter calls field.evaluate_cartesian once per point, which runs Python loops over 136 modes and a fresh scalar Legendre recurrence every call. The batch engine (trace_field_batch + evaluate_cartesian_batch) already gives identical results. In addition, execute_solar_physics_job builds a new SolarCoronaPhysicsModel, and with it a new empty PFSSCache, inside a fresh spawn worker for every request. The client also sends jd_tdb with 8 decimals. So the PFSS solution cache can never hit in the shipped path, and every request pays for decomposition, 120 scalar traces and 2592 WSA traces. |
| P023 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | PFSS cache can never be hit in the shipped path: every /solar/physics request spawns a fresh process and model and recomputes PFSS cold (12-13 s wall, ~13.7 s CPU), even for an identical epoch — execute_solar_physics_job builds SolarCoronaPhysicsModel(...) inside each spawn child, and the model constructor creates a new PFSSCache. The child exits after one job. So the bounded, single-flight PFSSCache and the synthetic snapshot cache never see a second request, and the API process has no result cache. PFSS dominates the cost: a warm in-process sample takes 0.02 s, a cold one 7.7 s at 'operational'. The shipped UI (fidelity=high, max_features=180, forcing=hybrid) polls every 30 s with the sim JD, so a paused sim re-requests the same epoch and pays the full cold cost each time. The plan's step 3 lists 'supervised subprocess isolation ... and cache-hit bypass'; isolation shipped, the cache-hit bypass did not. |
| P073 | this-audit status-incidental-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | UNVERIFIED | Process isolation discarded all PFSS result reuse: identical /solar/physics requests re-solve cold (~16 s) every time — Each request spawns a fresh child that builds a new model, so the in-process PFSSCache is never reused (historical warm hit ~7-9 us). Each open tab pays a full cold solve on the UI's default high-fidelity poll every 30 s. |
| P024 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Solar process queue admits jobs that cannot finish: queued /solar/physics requests always end in 503 solar_compute_timeout after ~17 s while using a child's CPU — The 18 s absolute deadline starts at submit(), so it includes time spent in the queue. A shipped-shape job takes 11-17 s. A job in one of the Q=2 queue slots waits for a running child to finish, then spawns a new child with only a few seconds left. _execute only refuses to start if the deadline has already passed, so it spawns the child and then kills it. The client gets 503 solar_compute_timeout with retryable=true after ~17 s, which invites a retry that repeats the pattern. |
| P074 | this-audit status-incidental-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | UNVERIFIED | Queued solar jobs inherit the admission-time deadline, so with high fidelity (~16 s) every queued request times out after burning CPU — The deadline is fixed at admission. A queued high-fidelity job starts only after a running one finishes (~16-17 s), which leaves ~1-2 s before the 18 s hard kill. Queue slots therefore return 503 solar_compute_timeout instead of results. |
| P025 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | GONG body-read deadline is only checked after a blocking read returns; a slow-drip body holds one read(64 KiB) far past read_timeout_s and the total acquisition deadline — _BoundedHttpResponse.read sets the socket timeout to min(remaining, stall) and calls HTTPResponse.read(size). http.client reads through a BufferedReader, which keeps calling recv() until it has 'size' bytes or reaches EOF. The socket timeout limits each recv, not the whole call. A peer sending one byte every less-than-stall seconds can therefore keep a single read(64 KiB) blocked for up to 65,536 x stall seconds (about 3.8 days with the 5 s default). read_timeout_s and the total deadline in _AttemptBudget are only checked after the call returns, and the error is labelled socket_stall_timeout even though no recv stalled. The tests use a fake clock and a fake raw response, so they check only the label afterwards and cannot see the blocking. |
| P016 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | WSA expansion-factor tests are invariant under fs -> 1/fs: an inverted fs mutant passes all 1110 PFSS/WSA tests while turning almost every open cell into max-speed wind — Every fs assertion uses a RadialTube with Br ~ 1/r^2. For that field (1/Rss)^2*Br(1)/Br(Rss) == 1 == Rss^2*Br(Rss)/Br(1), so the tests cannot tell fs from 1/fs. No test evaluates fs on a real PFSS field, although the dipole has a closed form (field lines follow (2/r+q r^2) sin^2 th = const). The R4-WSA-RADIAL-COMPONENT gate only distinguishes the radial component from the vector magnitude. |
| P017 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | Surviving numerical mutants: RK4 weights/stage offsets, hard-coded Rss=2.5 in the batch evaluator, and re-including the l=0 monopole all pass the full PFSS suite — The tracer tests use radial, constant or linear fields, where any consistent integrator is exact. Integrator order and weights are therefore never checked against a curved analytic field (dipole conjugate footpoints or flux-function invariance). All analytic-field tests use r_ss=2.5, so a batch evaluator that ignores self.r_ss goes unnoticed, even though PFSSSolutionConfig accepts any Rss>1. ADR 0003 says a supplied g00 is excluded, but no test passes g00 to the solver. |
| P019 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | UNVERIFIED | WSA source-surface lookup structurally under-samples the heliospheric-current-sheet band because field lines are traced up from a photospheric grid; at the activity floor ~20% of Parker arms (100% at activity 0) fall back to the empirical model — Traces start from a uniform 36x72 photospheric grid. Open flux near coronal-hole boundaries spreads over the low-latitude source surface, so few samples land near the HCS, and the lookup only accepts samples within 2 cell diagonals. Operational WSA traces down from a uniform source-surface grid instead. |
| P022 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | GONG flux-balance gate rejects 100% of real zqs maps; the exactly-balanced synthetic fixture hides it — _balance_flux requires \|signed flux\| <= max(1e-12*unsigned, 1e-12*4pi) ('roundoff-only'). The plan (lines 107-112) assumes zqs maps arrive already balanced. PFSSCache._validate_observed_flux re-applies the same limit. Real GONG zqs maps are float32 and carry a net monopole of 2-5% of unsigned flux, about 1e10 times the limit. parse_gong_fits therefore raises flux_unbalanced for every real file, after all header and WCS gates have passed. The only fixture is built from paired +/-d raw values that cancel exactly, so no test can show the assumption is false. |
| P026 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | The observed-snapshot parser has no physical plausibility bounds: an all-zero map or a 1e4x mis-scaled map is accepted as 'observed' and solved — After the structural and WCS gates, parse_gong_fits only checks that values are finite and that the net flux is within the monopole limit. An all-zero map (or BSCALE=0) passes the flux gate trivially, and any BUNIT equivalent to gauss (T, mT) is silently rescaled. There is no bound on \|B\|, on unsigned flux, or on the fraction of zero pixels. |
| P027 | this-audit discovery-2026-10-09 / 2026-10-09 | OPEN | One slow child reap breaks /solar/physics until the server restarts (quarantine has no recovery path except shutdown) — _terminate_and_reap gives terminate and kill 0.25 s each. If the child is still alive after that, it raises ProcessReapFailed and _quarantine_job sets _broken_reason, so every later submit raises ProcessSupervisorBroken. Nothing re-checks the child after it does exit. Only shutdown() retries the reap, and _get_solar_physics_runner will not replace a runner that is broken but not closed. |

| B010 | /home/nomad/ai/projects/repositories/solar-system-realistic-sim/agent-notes/BUG_FIX_REPORT_2026-10-17.md:94 / 04d6e3791ca43135a22f3fb8c6fa6aa7e2259f71f8561526902918757e88a8a5 | FIX_PRESENT_BASELINE_NOT_INDEPENDENTLY_RECHECKED_HERE | #### B010 — Cargo bisection never terminates (my PR #3) - **Where:** `backend/mission/vehicle_service.py:195-207` (`max_closable_cargo_kg`), fed by   `mining_service.py:34-42` and `agents.py:209-216`. - **Mechanism:**   - `while hi - lo > tolerance_kg` has no iteration cap and no PlanningContext checkpoint.   - With `available_cargo_kg = inf` (finite HTTP inputs reach it: `available_power_kw: 1e308` / 0.24 overflows), `hi`     stays `inf` forever.   - Above about 9e15 kg the float spacing exceeds the 1 kg tolerance, so `mid` collapses onto `lo` or `hi` and the loop     never ends. - **Impact:**   - The request itself returns 504 at the deadline.   - Its compute thread spins forever and keeps the **only** mission permit, so every later `/mission/plan` gets     `503 mission_plan_saturated` until restart.   - It also takes one of the two shared heavy-compute threads. - **Evidence:** `out/scratch/mission-r1/repro_bisect_hang.py` → `deliverable inf`, `alive after 5 s: True`, 577,971   `evaluate_burn_budget` calls. `http_bisect_hang.py` → 504, then 503 for valid requests. - **Fix:**   - Reject a non-finite `available_cargo_kg`.   - Bound the loop (`for _ in range(200)`), and break when `mid` is not strictly between `lo` and `hi`.   - Check the PlanningContext inside the loop.   - Cap `extraction_rate_kg_day`, `available_power_kw` and `mining_days` in `MissionPlanRequest` to physical maxima,     so that inf cannot be produced. - **Test (red first):** `max_closable_cargo_kg(..., available_cargo_kg=math.inf)` returns or raises within 1 s; HTTP   `/mission/plan` with `1e308` mining inputs gives 422 and leaves the permit free.  |
| B011 | /home/nomad/ai/projects/repositories/solar-system-realistic-sim/agent-notes/BUG_FIX_REPORT_2026-10-17.md:95 / 04d6e3791ca43135a22f3fb8c6fa6aa7e2259f71f8561526902918757e88a8a5 | FIX_PRESENT_BASELINE_NOT_INDEPENDENTLY_RECHECKED_HERE | #### B011 — `/ws/sim` blocks the event loop for ~2 s per handshake - **Where:** `backend/server.py:5011-5041`. `_serve_simulation_websocket` is `async`, but it builds the engine and calls   `engine.initialize(ALL_BODIES)` (~2.0 s of CPU) inline. - **Origin:** the inline call is old, but it was cheap (1 ms on `origin/main`). Remediation commit `2005a1f` made   `REBOUNDEngine.initialize` integrate the initial conditions (two `sim.integrate` calls, 2.07 s in total per   cProfile). A red-first test therefore fails only on the remediation line, not on a branch cut from `origin/main`. - **Evidence:** `out/scratch/srv-routes-r1/ws_block.py <backend>`: baseline `/health/live` 1.2 ms; during one   handshake, n=91 probes, **max 2,020 ms**. - **Impact:** any client freezes every HTTP route and WebSocket stream for ~2 s per connect. A reconnect loop keeps the   API mostly frozen, and the 4-slot cap doesn't help because each slot is released quickly. - **Fix:** move engine selection, construction, `initialize` and the three initial reads into one sync helper, and run   it with `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` inside the admission slot. Ownership passes to the runner thread only after it   returns, so it stays sequential. - **Test:** a TestClient/uvicorn probe asserting `/health/live` max latency < 200 ms during a handshake; or a fake   engine asserting `initialize` runs off the event-loop thread.  |

That commit changed the old check (`ok === true && !isRecord(sdo_aia)` → "…sdo_aia status claims success but snapshot data is unavailable") into the biconditional, and added two new `it.each` blocks (test.ts:180-210) with the new message, but left the older table row. Four more commits (477030a 03:11, 2620db9 03:13, 774cb89 03:29, 17d1e63 03:30) landed on a red suite.   Which side is right: the validator. Backend contract: `_fetch_snapshot_with_deadline` writes `snapshot["sdo_aia"]=<dict>` and `source_status.sdo_aia.ok=True` together (2612-2618), or `ok:False,error` and leaves `sdo_aia=None` (2624-2629), so "ok ⇔ payload non-null" is the true invariant; the new check also rejects the opposite contradiction (ok:false + payload) that the old one allowed. The row's payload (ok:true, `sdo_aia:null`) is still rejected for the *same* semantic reason ("success claimed, no data"); only the wording changed. The earlier check order is irrelevant: schema/source/`source_status` per-source checks all pass first (I read the call order, lines 555-596), so the mismatch check is the first to fire (matches the CI message).   Verified fix on the copy: `sed -i "589s/'sdo_aia status'/'source_status.sdo_aia.ok must match'/" …test.ts` → `Tests 60 passed (60)`; with `solarPhysicsClient`, `solarMagnetics`, `sunController` tests → 89/89. - Impact: `npm test` fails 1/309 (CI step 1 of the only workflow), so the R3/R4 science manifest and typecheck ratchet steps never run; the suite was already red at each of the 4 later commits. - Fix: one line, `solarRealtimeClient.test.ts:589` → `'source_status.sdo_aia.ok must match'`. Optional hardening: the row is now redundant with test.ts:196-211 (same payload class); delete it or assert a stable error code instead of prose. - Prior: NEW (baseline CI fact; root cause here) - Adversarial check: tried to find a different reason the payload should be rejected (e.g. an earlier validation step with a different message): none fires first. Tried changing the validator message instead: would break the dedicated test at :208 which expects the new text, so the test-side change is the minimal consistent one. 59/60 other rows pass, so no wider drift.  |
| F-SOL-02 | git:0bbc1c09995af48d6b46ebd01b275216358601cb:agent-notes/CODEBASE_EVALUATION_REPORT_2026-10-06_APPENDIX_B_REVIEWERS.md:79 / 29560a0d1a6aae61dce5040c21d448c12a41fd07da97dcb9cabc2844c6960004 | PENDING_SEMANTIC_REVIEW | ### F-SOL-02 — The Sun's default `/solar/physics` request (`high`, 180 features) needs ~34 s CPU against a hard 18 s backend deadline - Severity: High   - Class: VERIFIED (measured on this 4-core 2.8 GHz Xeon VM; other hardware may differ, see adversarial check)   - Reach: LIVE + BACKEND   - Effort: S (frontend parameter) / M (adaptive client) - Where: src/sunController.ts:171-177 (`fidelity: 'high'`, `maxFeatures: 180`); src/frontend/features/solar/solarPhysicsClient.ts:9-10,214-218,286,329 (30 s cadence, locked 20 s timeout, `jd_tdb` to 8 decimals, 30 s retry); backend/server.py:912-924 (18.0 s hard deadline); backend/sim/solar_process_worker.py `execute_solar_physics_job` - Evidence:   ```   $ curl -m 60 'http://127.0.0.1:18143/solar/physics?jd_tdb=2461320.00000000&fidelity=high&max_features=180&forcing=hybrid&live_data=true'   http=503 time_total=18.0156   {"detail":{"code":"solar_compute_timeout","message":"Solar physics generation exceeded its hard deadline.",…}}   (repeated: 18.0259 s)   $ python time_physics2.py high 180      -> wall=36.74s cpu=34.42s      (process CPU time, so not a load artefact)     …                       operational 180 -> cpu=18.54s ; preview 180 -> cpu=8.54s ; high 32 -> cpu=38.39s (cost is set by fidelity, not feature count)   $ curl …fidelity=preview…  -> http=200 size_download=356550 time_total=10.63 (no Content-Encoding; no GZip middleware, server.py:1349-1380)   ```   The client sends `jd_tdb=Number(jd).toFixed(8)` of the live sim JD, so no two requests share an epoch and nothing can be cached. A failed attempt is retried 30 s after it fails (`solarPhysicsClient.ts:329` `max(30 s, pollInterval)`, constant, no exponential backoff); `ctrl/harness_down.ts` (instant 503s, 600 s of 60 fps frames) shows exactly that cadence (requests at 0, 30, 60 … s). With the real 18 s deadline that is one attempt per ≈48 s, i.e. ≈18 s of worker CPU per 48 s (≈37 % of a core per open tab; computed from the measured 18.0 s deadline and the 30 s retry, not measured end to end).   One extra observation (cause not established): a `preview` request issued right after the two `high` timeouts also returned `solar_compute_timeout` after only 9.26 s; two later `preview` requests were 200. Candidate: the 0.25 s child-exit grace (`process_supervisor.py:36,459-466`) under load.   When it does succeed the payload is 712,225 B compact (corona 65 %, pfss 30 %, heliosphere 4 %; every large section is consumed by the frontend), i.e. 23.7 KB/s per tab at the 30 s cadence. - Impact: on hardware like this VM (and, per the baseline, the GitHub runner: five `503 solar_compute_timeout` backend test failures) the physics state is never delivered, so the Sun silently runs on its local synthetic fallback; the UI has no indicator of this (index.html has no backend/synthetic status text) and the tab keeps asking the server to start work that is killed at the deadline. - Fix: (1) `sunController.ts:173-174` → `fidelity: 'preview'` (8.5 s CPU) or `'operational'` only where the backend is known to finish; (2) in `SolarPhysicsClient` map `solar_compute_timeout`/`solar_compute_saturated` to a step-down (`high→operational→preview`) plus exponential backoff (the realtime client already has one); (3) backend: quantise the epoch (e.g. 0.01 d) so identical requests hit a cache, and enable compression (≈60 % smaller); (4) show "Solar physics: synthetic fallback" in the status bar. - Prior: K-11 (CHANGED: cadence fixed 900 ms → 30 s by 8236061; payload now larger; new deadline failure) - Adversarial check: tried to blame CPU contention (load average ≈6 on 4 cores): the measurement is process CPU time (34.4 s) with `nice`, and `Thread(s) per core: 1`, so contention cannot double it; `SOLAR_PHYSICS_COMPUTE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` cannot exceed 19 s (`server.py:912`), so no configuration makes `high` pass here. A machine ≥2× faster would pass `high`, which is why this is "environment-sensitive High" rather than Critical; the repo's own backend gate ("Real gates cover high/180", `process_supervisor.py:28-30`) fails in CI for the same reason.  |

All five deadline CI failures reproduce in isolation (F-API-03). `/solar/capabilities` advertises `["preview","operational","high","ultra"]` with no latency information (`server.py:3004-3009`). - Impact: with the backend running as the README says, the sun layer never receives a response at the frontend's default settings. Every 30 s (`solarPhysicsClient.ts:9-11`) the backend burns up to 18 CPU-s and then kills the child (≈60 % duty cycle of one core, indefinitely) for nothing. Two of the four admitted slots are queue slots whose clock starts at admission (`process_supervisor.py:253-289`, `test_solar_process_supervisor.py:97`), so a queued job gets only the remainder of 18 s and is killed mid-compute. There is no operator remedy: `SOLAR_PHYSICS_COMPUTE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` is clamped to 19 s (`server.py:912,915-921`, asserted by `test_solar_process_endpoint.py:302-311`) and undocumented. Five CI tests fail for this reason. - Fix: (1) stop paying the cold PFSS cost per request — keep one long-lived worker process per slot holding a warm `SolarCoronaPhysicsModel` (restart it on timeout/kill), or persist the PFSS solution content-addressed by the existing `solution_id` so a fresh child can load it (measured 8.3 s → 0.01 s); decide with the solar reviewer whether the synthetic solution identity really needs the exact epoch, because the frontend polls with a moving `jd_tdb` (`solarPhysicsClient.ts:286`) and an exact-epoch cache would still miss every poll; (2) add a parent-side response cache + single-flight keyed by `(epoch, fidelity, max_features, forcing, live_data)`; (3) make the contract honest until (1) lands — per-fidelity deadlines with the browser timeout raised to match (`solarPhysicsClient.ts:10`, `server.py:912`), or change `sunController.ts:171-176` to `operational`/`preview`; (4) for queued jobs, start the deadline at dequeue or reject with `solar_compute_saturated` when predicted wait + cost exceeds the budget; (5) add a gate that runs every advertised fidelity through the real runner with the production deadline (the existing wire-budget test would have been the place). - Prior: NEW (K-11's 900 ms poll is fixed — poll is now 30 s — which makes the permanent failure quieter, not absent). - Adversarial check: (a) "this box is just slow/loaded" — the claim rests on CPU-seconds (30 s user) not wall; the GitHub `ubuntu-24.04` runner fails the same five tests (run 36307010887); this VM runs the 1e7-iteration Python loop in 0.65–0.78 s, while a modern laptop core typically needs roughly 0.4–0.6 s (my estimate, not measured), i.e. ≈1.2–2× faster — so `high` would still need ≈15–25 CPU-s there against 18 s, with no headroom for two parallel workers or a browser rendering on the same machine. Even if shared-core (SMT) contention inflated my CPU-seconds by 1.5× — plausible on 4 shared vCPUs, not measured — `high/180` would still be ≈20 s. `operational` is the borderline case: the CI runner also failed the default-parameter test (`test_jd_inside_the_window_is_accepted`, operational/220), so it does not fit there either. (b) "the frontend degrades gracefully" — true (30 s back-off, no crash), which is why this is High not Critical; the feature simply never delivers while burning CPU. (c) "a mocked timeout" — no: the 503 comes from the real supervisor at 18.0 s with a real child. (d) "an env override exists" — clamped at 19 s. Outcome: stands.  |

It also muddies diagnosis of F-API-01 because both surface as the same error code. - Fix: decode and validate first (`self._decode_result(encoded, payload)`), return the result, and let the existing `finally` (`:477-491`, `_reap_or_quarantine`) terminate/join the child; never convert an already-validated result into an error. Add a test whose target sleeps 0.6 s after sending. - Prior: NEW. - Adversarial check: could the child have been genuinely over its deadline? No — the two HTTP failures occurred at ≈9.5 s of an 18 s budget and the direct run printed the discard message; the 1.5× margin measured in `exit_delay.py` is thin and varies with heap size (the child holds numpy/astropy structures).  |

Over real transport 160 early-drop attempts (RST/FIN, with and without reading the 101) left 9 threads constant (presumably because nothing yields between `accept()` and the first send on this uvicorn 0.52.4 / websockets 17 stack — my inference, not instrumented). a single batched call gives identical results in 3.9 s) - Severity: High   - Class: VERIFIED   - Reach: LIVE (shipped UI polls `fidelity:'high'`, `forcing:'hybrid'` every 30 s)   - Effort: S (batch the lines) + S/M (rest) - Where: `backend/sim/pfss_magnetogram.py:417-470` (loop, scalar call at :446); `backend/sim/pfss_tracing.py:239-254` (`trace_field` = batch of one + `field.evaluate_cartesian` per point); `backend/sim/solar_process_worker.py:94` (new model + `PFSSCache` per job); `backend/server.py:912-924` (18 s default, 19 s hard max); `src/sunController.ts:171-177` - Evidence:   ```   e2e_solar_http.py (TestClient, real spawn workers, loadavg 2.4)   GET /solar/physics fidelity=preview      -> HTTP 200 in 10.0s   GET /solar/physics fidelity=operational  -> HTTP 503 in 18.0s solar_compute_timeout   (server default)   GET /solar/physics fidelity=high         -> HTTP 503 in 18.0s solar_compute_timeout   (what the UI sends)   solar_cost2.py, lmax=15, 120 lines:  trace_field_lines 25.9 s CPU \| compute_wsa_velocity_map(36x72) 10.7 s \| decompose 0.01 s   trace_batch_vs_scalar.py:  scalar-per-line 28.4 s CPU   vs   one trace_field_batch(120, record_arcs=True) 3.8 s                              states agree 120/120, max endpoint diff 2.6e-15 R_sun, step counts equal 120/120   fix_proof_batch_lines.py (monkeypatched trace_field_lines):  operational 18.1 -> 9.2 s,  high 32.0 -> 13.7 s CPU   ``` - Impact: the same symptom is reported as F-SOL-02 (UI never gets the physics state) and as five CI failures (F-REPO-11); this finding is the cause and the cheap fix. The placeholder "blend" references one hour earlier were round numbers (`ACCURACY_REPORT_2026-02-15_04-51-05.md:17-19`: 8.600 / 7.200 / 17.000); the "strict" consensus values are 8.490 / 7.108 / 16.873 (−1.3 %, −1.3 %, −0.7 %). | F-TRJ-02 | git:0bbc1c09995af48d6b46ebd01b275216358601cb:agent-notes/CODEBASE_EVALUATION_REPORT_2026-10-06_APPENDIX_B_REVIEWERS.md:1124 / 29560a0d1a6aae61dce5040c21d448c12a41fd07da97dcb9cabc2844c6960004 | PENDING_SEMANTIC_REVIEW | ### F-TRJ-02 — Mission planner: payload closure and risk model give inverted answers; the default request can never succeed and its 422 hides why - Severity: High   - Class: VERIFIED   - Reach: BACKEND (`POST /mission/plan`, README:19,301-305; no shipped UI calls it)   - Effort: M - Where: `backend/mission/mining_service.py:77-81`; `backend/mission/agents.py:480-486,495-501,531-533`; `backend/mission/risk_service.py:65-69,35-37`; `backend/mission/vehicle_service.py:154-162`; `backend/server.py:4104-4109` - Evidence:   ```   mining_service.py:81   returned_payload_kg = max(0.0, delivered_before_propellant - return_propellant_kg)   agents.py:533          score = float(closure["returnedPayloadKg"]) - float(logistics.get("totalPropellantUsedKg", 0.0)) - risk_penalty - time_penalty   risk_service.py:65-66  margin_penalty = (dv - base_total_delta_v_km_s) * 120.0                          margin_penalty += max(0.0, base_returned_payload_kg - payload) * 0.08   ```   `POST /mission/plan {}` → **HTTP 422** `{"code":"mission_no_feasible_recommendation","message":"no_verified_candidate","context":{}}` (the `alternatives` with their `verification.reasons` are computed and then discarded at `server.py:4104-4109`). Direct `MissionPlannerAgent.plan({})` (`mission_default2.py`): every candidate is `vehicle_budget_not_feasible` with **unmet Δv 46.26 km/s** (outbound 28.12 + return 21.85 km/s), propellant burns `[23970, 0]` kg, yet `returnedPayloadKg = 9,499` (= storable cargo − 0 kg return propellant), `failureProbability = 0.000`, `missionScore = −14,666`. Default vehicle total capability measured by bisection on `VehicleService`: **3.716 km/s** (initial mass 41,100 kg) versus ≥ 11.2 km/s for the cheapest Earth→Mars→Earth (5.6 + 5.6 v∞ sums) → no date makes the default request succeed.   The opposite case (`mission_closing2.py`: extra-heavy vehicle that *does* close, Earth→Mars→Earth, dep JD 2461344.5, mining 250 d): burns 6.45 / 6.49 km/s using 967,389 / 153,370 kg, storable cargo 10,335 kg → `returnedPayloadKg = max(0, 9,922 − 153,370) = 0`, `failureProbability = 1.0`, verification `no_returned_payload`. So infeasible ⇒ full cargo + P(fail) 0; feasible ⇒ zero cargo + P(fail) 1. The only success the repo's tests exercise (`test_mission_agents.py:14-51`) uses two 100-kg-dry-mass stages carrying 2,000 t of propellant at Isp 1000 s, 5,000 mining days at 50,000 kg/day, 100 % yield and a failure threshold of 1.0.   K-31 items re-verified: mined cargo is never added to the mass in the rocket equation (`agents.py:480-486` passes only `payload_mass_kg`; cargo enters only afterwards in `close_payload`), the return propellant is deducted from cargo (`mining_service.py:81`) and then total propellant (including that same return burn) is deducted again in the score (`agents.py:533`). Rocket-equation mechanics themselves are correct (`vehicle_service.py:87-104`: `ve = isp*G0`, `Δm = m0(1−e^{−Δv/ve})`, staging drops dry mass + reserve). Risk constants are invented: margin penalty 120 kg per km/s of Δv overrun versus the rocket-equation sensitivity of the default vehicle `m0/ve = 11,642 kg per km/s` (97× smaller), `risk_penalty = 9000·P(fail)` and `time_penalty = 0.25·days` (kg vs days) at `agents.py:531-532`, σ fractions 1 %/4 %/12 % at `risk_service.py:35-37` with no source. Monte-Carlo itself is deterministic (`random.Random(seed+idx)`; same seed ⇒ identical failureProbability and score; `determinism.py` identical across 3 hash seeds). - Impact: The module's three advertised outputs (payload-return closure, risk envelopes, verified recommendation) are wrong for every realistic input and right only for contrived ones; the HTTP API gives a client no way to learn why. Any decision log or score from this endpoint is meaningless. - Fix: (1) `agents.py:480-501`: give `VehicleService.evaluate_burn_budget` a per-burn `mass_added_before_burn_kg` list and pass `[0, storable_cargo × handling_survival]` for the return burn; (2) `mining_service.py:63-90`: stop subtracting vehicle propellant from cargo (returned = cargo × survival); (3) `agents.py:533`: score with returned payload minus *non-recoverable* cost only (or remove the propellant term entirely) and put each constant behind a named, documented parameter; (4) `risk_service.py:65-69`: make a candidate with `logistics.feasible == False` fail by construction and derive the margin sensitivity from the vehicle (`m/ve`) instead of 120; (5) `server.py:4104-4109`: put `alternatives[*].verification.reasons` into the 422 `context`; (6) change the defaults (`vehicle_service.py:154-162` and the default departure JD) to something that can close, with a test that `POST /mission/plan {}` returns 200. - Prior: K-31 (STILL-PRESENT, lines moved), K-52 risk model + default 422 (STILL-PRESENT). - Adversarial check: Could the "carved out of cargo" rule be an ISRU-propellant model? Then (i) the vehicle's own propellant would not also be charged in `agents.py:533` (double count), (ii) the infeasible case would not report full cargo with zero return propellant, and (iii) P(fail) would not ignore logistics feasibility — all three observed. Could the 422 be the correct "guard" outcome? The verifier does stop a wrong *recommendation* from being returned, but it is stopping everything realistic, and the discarded alternatives show P(fail)=0.000 for infeasible plans. Reachable? Yes — live endpoint, only the (unreachable) UI is missing. Survives as High.  |

| F-TRJ-11 | git:0bbc1c09995af48d6b46ebd01b275216358601cb:agent-notes/CODEBASE_EVALUATION_REPORT_2026-10-06_APPENDIX_B_REVIEWERS.md:1244 / 29560a0d1a6aae61dce5040c21d448c12a41fd07da97dcb9cabc2844c6960004 | PARTIAL_CONFIRMED_CURRENT_BUG_AND_SEARCH_LIMITATIONS; see fresh facet register | ### F-TRJ-11 — Containment residuals: sustained duty cycle, biased truncation, advertised grid cap unreachable - Severity: Low   - Class: VERIFIED   - Reach: BACKEND   - Effort: S - Where: `backend/server.py:1050-1055` (60 req/min), `:2586-2623` (unique-state check), `:3543-3546` (capabilities); `backend/trajectory/lambert.py:989-1002` (row-major scan) - Evidence: per-request limits genuinely hold (see Strengths), but (a) the rate limit is 60/min per peer while one worst-case porkchop costs 1.07 s CPU, so one peer can keep one core ≈ 100 % busy (`/health/live` median latency 2.1 ms idle → 41–75 ms median, p95 ≈ 150 ms under 3 hammering clients, `health_under_load.py`/`hang_probe2.py`); (b) when the deadline fires the scan stops row-major, so a truncated porkchop contains only the earliest departures (`deadline_test.py`: 265 of 1,881 cells, `best` = best of the first 265 only) and the response is HTTP 200 with `truncated:true` — correct flag, but `best` is not window-best; (c) `/trajectory/capabilities` advertises `maxPorkchopGridPoints: 2000` but `server.py:2608-2623` requires `D + D·T ≤ 2000`: a 100×20 grid is rejected with 413 "exceeds the unique-state computation budget", the largest near-square grid is 99×19 = 1,881. One unreproduced observation: in 2 of my first 6 sustained-load runs a client saw no response for ≥ 20 s on one request; 25 further runs (≈ 8,000 requests, with thread-dump instrumentation) showed none, so I treat it as harness/CPU-contention noise (the machine was at load ≈ 7 on 4 cores). - Impact: none exploitable; documentation/limits drift only. - Fix: scan departures in a strided order (or coarse-to-fine) in `scan_porkchop_window` so a truncated result samples the whole window; publish `maxPorkchopCells = floor(2000/(1+T))` in capabilities or relax the unique-state estimate; add a per-peer CPU-seconds budget to `_TrajectoryRateLimitMiddleware` if the server ever binds beyond loopback. - Prior: K-52 ("porkchop CPU unbounded") FIXED-ON-HEAD.  |

| F-FEC-02 | git:0bbc1c09995af48d6b46ebd01b275216358601cb:agent-notes/CODEBASE_EVALUATION_REPORT_2026-10-06_APPENDIX_B_REVIEWERS.md:1383 / 29560a0d1a6aae61dce5040c21d448c12a41fd07da97dcb9cabc2844c6960004 | PENDING_SEMANTIC_REVIEW | ### F-FEC-02 — Node precession has the wrong sign for retrograde moons (285 mean-element moons + Triton) - Severity: **Medium**  - Class: VERIFIED  - Reach: LIVE-GATED (`showMoons=false`) / DATA  - Effort: S (code) + M (re-baseline gate) - Where: `src/sim/catalog.ts:442-468,474-475`; budgets that hide it `src/sim/moonFrameCheck.ts:163,171-173,283-285`; data `src/data/moons.json`. - Evidence:   ```ts   const argRate  = precessionRateDegreesPerCentury(moon.apsisPrecessionYears, 1,  moon.periodDays);   const nodeRate = precessionRateDegreesPerCentury(moon.nodePrecessionYears, -1, moon.periodDays); // same sign for i=28° and i=157°   ```   287/424 records have i>90° and *all* carry a positive `nodePrecessionYears`, so all get Ω̇<0 (285 ecliptic irregulars + Triton + Phoebe; Phoebe uses the fit). Physics: for a retrograde orbit Ω̇ ∝ −cos i > 0 (e.g. solar quadrupole, Pasiphae: +3.3°/yr vs table magnitude 4.5°/yr). Against the repo's own Horizons fixture (plane-normal error, deg, at `j2000 p30d p180d p1y p5y 2025 2026`; `node retro_check.mjs`):   ```   Pasiphae  shipped 8.2 7.9 8.6 10.7 19.5 50.9 49.4 \| node sign flipped 8.2 7.9 8.0 8.3 6.0 7.7 7.3   Sinope    shipped 5.2 5.4 4.3  5.2 12.5 42.0 42.7 \| node sign flipped 5.2 5.4 4.1 3.5 3.6 3.5 2.1   Carme     shipped 0.1 0.6 2.2  3.5  9.5 30.2 30.8 \| node sign flipped 0.1 0.5 1.2 1.4 1.3 1.6 3.2   Himalia (prograde control) shipped 2.3° @2025 \| flipped 26.3°   Triton shipped 14.6° \| flipped 5.6° \| +0.5x\|table\| 0.49°   ```   The gate budgets for these rows are 101.9°, 84.0°, 61.7° (Pasiphae/Sinope/Carme) and 20° (Triton), justified in prose as "solar-perturbed, non-Keplerian" — i.e. they are sized to the bug. Applying the one-line repair (sign = −sign(cos i)) in a scratch copy makes the repo's gate **fail** (`Carme @2025: 4.786e7 km > 3.4e7`, `Triton @2025: 2.140e5 > 2.0e5`) even though plane error improves 7-19x, because position budgets were calibrated to the buggy output and phase (mean-motion, F-FEC-03) dominates position error. - Impact: if moons are ever switched on, 68% of the catalog's orbit planes precess the wrong way (planes 30-51° off by 2025 for the three fixture irregulars); the CI gate cannot see it and rejects the fix. Triton additionally needs \|rate\| ≈ 0.5x the table value (best fit +52.9°/cy vs table 105.8°/cy). - Fix: `catalog.ts:475` use `(moon.inclinationDeg ?? 0) > 90 ? +1 : -1` for the node direction; re-baseline `POSITION_BUDGET_KM`/`PLANE_BUDGET_DEG` rows for Pasiphae/Sinope/Carme/Triton to measured-with-fix values (plane budgets ≤10°); for Triton prefer adding it to `generate_moon_ephemeris.py` `TARGETS` (Horizons fit) over rate-tweaking. - Prior: NEW (K-49/K-05 family; the apsis sign was tested and should stay +1: flipping both made e-vector error worse at 5 yr, 69°/55°/83° vs 10°/8°/12°). - Adversarial check: refute attempts — (1) sign handled elsewhere? `resolveKeplerOrbitAtElapsedDays`/`sourceFrameOrbit` apply the rate as given; (2) JPL table might already be signed? 0 of 424 negative; (3) maybe truth is non-Keplerian? Flipping lowers plane error 7-19x for all three independent retrograde irregulars while a prograde control (Himalia) gets worse — a sign effect, not noise. Positions do **not** improve (phase lost: documented 2.4-3.9% mean-rate errors), so I claim plane-normal only. Reach is gated off, hence Medium not High.  |

| F-FEC-13 | git:0bbc1c09995af48d6b46ebd01b275216358601cb:agent-notes/CODEBASE_EVALUATION_REPORT_2026-10-06_APPENDIX_B_REVIEWERS.md:1533 / 29560a0d1a6aae61dce5040c21d448c12a41fd07da97dcb9cabc2844c6960004 | PENDING_SEMANTIC_REVIEW | ### F-FEC-13 — Planet spin axes do not follow IAU poles; Venus, Uranus and Pluto rotate the wrong way - Severity: **Medium**  - Class: VERIFIED (vector math + Three.js transform replicated; not visually probed)  - Reach: LIVE (visible on Earth/Mars/Sun surfaces)  - Effort: S-M - Where: `src/main.ts:308-318,722-737`, `src/data/planets.ts` (`axialTiltDeg` / `spinAxisLongitudeDeg` / `rotationPeriodHours`). - Evidence (`spin_vec.mjs`, `spin_sense.mjs`): angle between the scene's angular-velocity vector and IAU WGCCRE-2015 (pole RA/Dec, sign of dW/dt):   ```   sun 1.8°  mercury 7.0°  venus 176.2°  earth 32.7°  mars 2.2°  jupiter 4.5°  saturn 1.3°  uranus 15.5°  neptune 18.9°  pluto 111.3°   ```   `spinAxisLongitudeDeg` is set only for Saturn and Uranus; every other planet gets longitude 0 (Earth's true pole azimuth is +90°, so its tilt points at the vernal equinox instead of the solstice direction). Retrograde rotators encode the same fact twice (obliquity > 90° *and* a negative `rotationPeriodHours`), so Venus, Uranus and Pluto end up with angular velocity z>0 (prograde seen from ecliptic north: Venus `ω = (-0.046, 0, +0.999)`) whereas truth is retrograde. - Impact: Earth's day/night terminator vs. seasons are three months out of phase and the Earth/Mars/Sun surface features rotate about the wrong axis; `README:247` claims "correct ecliptic-longitude pole directions". - Fix: store IAU `poleRaDeg/poleDecDeg` per planet in `planets.ts` and derive the world pole with the existing `equatorialToEcliptic()` (as `PARENT_EQUATOR_POLE_OVERRIDE_ECLIPTIC` already does for Uranus/Pluto in `catalog.ts:130-133`); encode retrograde only through the sign of `rotationPeriodHours`; add a vitest comparing the ten axes to a 10-row IAU table (<0.1°). - Prior: K-07 note "spinAxisLongitudeDeg never read" is out of date (now read at `main.ts:310`) but the data stays wrong.  |

## External acceptance boundaries

- Original-code licence and commercial/noncommercial distribution policy require an owner decision; third-party notices do not grant missing Deimos redistribution rights.
- Manual screen-reader and real-touch acceptance cannot be inferred from DOM tests. Remote TLS/auth/proxy acceptance requires a specified deployed target and authorization.
- Numerical regression success is separate from observed-provider calibration and scientific validation. Missing reference data cannot be replaced by a fabricated oracle.
- The current default visualization is the local simulation path; the retained SimulationClient is intentionally API/library-only. This audit does not silently change that product decision.
